entity_title: EU citizen: report presence within 10 days for a stay under 3 months
fact_text: As an EU citizen coming to Belgium for a stay of less than three months, you (and any accompanying family members) must report to the municipality where you are temporarily staying within 10 days of arriving; you then receive a 'declaration of presence' (Annex 3ter). Failing to report within the time limit can lead to a 200 euro administrative fine.
evidence_quote: If you are an EU citizen visiting Belgium for a stay of less than three months, you and any family members who are accompanying you or joining you must report to the municipality of the place where you will be temporarily staying within 10 days of arriving.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: EU free movement means an EU citizen has nothing to file on arrival in Belgium. Actually: even for a stay under three months you must report your presence to the municipality within 10 days and receive an Annex 3ter. Action required: report to your Brussels commune within 10 days of arrival.

entity_title: EU citizen: register with the municipality within 3 months (stay over 3 months)
fact_text: As an EU citizen wishing to stay in Belgium for more than three months, you must register with the municipality where you are staying within three months of arriving; if you do not apply for the registration certificate within that period, a 200 euro administrative fine may be imposed.
evidence_quote: If you wish to stay in Belgium for more than three months, then you must register with the municipality of the place where you are staying within three months of arriving in Belgium.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: an EU citizen can simply move to Belgium with no paperwork. Actually: for a stay over three months you must register at your municipality within three months of arrival, and missing the deadline risks a 200 euro fine. Action required: book the commune registration soon after arriving in Brussels.

entity_title: EU citizen registration certificate (Annex 8 / E card)
fact_text: As an EU citizen whose right of residence is recognised, the municipality issues a 'registration certificate' in the form of a paper Annex 8; you may instead request an electronic E card.
evidence_quote: If your right of residence is recognised, the municipality will issue you with a ‘registration certificate’ in the form of a paper copy of an Annex 8; if you prefer, you can also apply for an electronic E card at that time.

entity_title: EU employee: register in the foreigners' register before the residence card (Brussels)
fact_text: As an EU (or assimilated) citizen who wants to stay in Belgium for more than three months as an employee, you must register in the foreigners' register of your municipality (in Brussels, the City of Brussels) before obtaining a residence card.
evidence_quote: The citizen of the European Union or of an assimilated country who wishes to stay in Belgium for more than 3 months must register in the foreigners' register of their municipality before obtaining a residence card.

entity_title: Single permit (combined work + residence) for non-EU stays over 90 days
fact_text: As a non-EU (non-European) national who will work and reside in Belgium for more than 90 days, a combined fixed-term single permit — one authorisation covering both work and residence — must be applied for (via the employer) from the competent region or the German-speaking Community.
evidence_quote: Would you like to hire a non-European employee who will work and reside in Belgium for more than 90 days? If so, apply for a combined fixed-term permit from the region, or from the German-speaking Community, where the employee will be working.

entity_title: Non-EU foreigner: register at the municipal administration to establish residence (Brussels)
fact_text: As a non-EU (non-Belgian) national who wishes to establish residence in the City of Brussels, you must present yourself for registration at the municipal administration of the City of Brussels.
evidence_quote: You are a foreign citizen (non-Belgian) and you wish to establish your residence in the City of Brussels? Then you must present yourself for registration at the municipal administration of the City of Brussels.

entity_title: Must join a health insurance fund (mutualité) — EU
fact_text: Health care reimbursements and benefits in Belgium are paid by a health insurance fund (mutualité/mutualiteit); to be entitled to them you must join a mutuality.
evidence_quote: Les mutualités paient, sous notre contrôle, les prestations de santé et les indemnités. Pour y avoir droit, vous devez vous affilier à une mutualité.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: health cover is automatic once you work. Actually: in Belgium you must actively join a health insurance fund (mutualité/mutualiteit) to be entitled to reimbursement of medical costs and benefits. Action required: choose and join a mutuality after registering.

entity_title: EU citizen registration certificate (Anmeldebescheinigung)
fact_text: As an EU/EEA or Swiss citizen entitled under Union law to reside in Austria for more than three months, you receive, upon request, a 'registration certificate' (Anmeldebescheinigung) documenting your right of residence.
evidence_quote: EU citizens, who are entitled, in accordance with Union law, to reside in Austria for more than three months, receive, upon request, a ‘registration certificate’, as documentation of their right of residence in accordance with Union law.

entity_title: EU citizen: register the stay within four months of arrival
fact_text: As an EU/EEA or Swiss citizen staying in Austria for more than three months, your stay must be registered with the competent settlement authority within four months of arrival in Austria (to obtain the registration certificate).
evidence_quote: The stay must be registered with the competent settlement authority within four months of arrival in Austria.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: EU free movement means no registration in Austria. Actually: you must register your stay with the settlement authority within four months of arrival to receive the Anmeldebescheinigung. Action required: book the registration-certificate appointment (in Vienna, the MA 35 EEA Unit) within four months.

entity_title: Red-White-Red Card for skilled workers in shortage occupations (third-country)
fact_text: As a non-EU (third-country) national you may apply for a Red-White-Red Card as a Skilled Worker in a Shortage Occupation, valid for 24 months; the shortage-occupation route requires a binding job offer at the legally stipulated minimum pay and reaching at least 55 of 100 points on the eligibility criteria.
evidence_quote: As a third-country citizen, you may apply for a Red-White-Red Card as a Skilled Worker in a Shortage Occupation valid for 24 months

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: any job offer lets a non-EU worker move to Austria. Actually: the Red-White-Red Card is points-based (min. 55/100) and the shortage-occupation route needs a job on the annual shortage list at the minimum pay. Action required: check the current shortage-occupation list and your score before planning the move.

entity_title: EU Blue Card for highly qualified workers (third-country)
fact_text: As a non-EU (third-country) national you may be granted an EU Blue Card if you have completed a university/tertiary course of study of at least three years, hold a binding job offer of at least six months matching your education, and will earn at least the average gross annual income of full-time employees.
evidence_quote: As a third-country citizen you may be granted an EU Blue Card

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: the ordinary work permit is the only route. Actually: a university degree plus a qualifying salary can make you eligible for an EU Blue Card, with no points system, which carries stronger mobility rights. Action required: check whether the Blue Card fits better than the Red-White-Red Card.

entity_title: Residence registration (Meldezettel) within three days — EEA
fact_text: Anyone who takes up accommodation in a dwelling in Austria must register with the competent registration authority (residence registration / Meldezettel) within three days of moving into the accommodation.
evidence_quote: Anyone who takes up accommodation in a dwelling in Austria is required to register themselves

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: registering your EU residence is the only registration needed. Actually: separately, everyone taking up accommodation in Austria must file a residence registration (Meldezettel) with the registration authority within three days of moving in. Action required: file the Meldezettel within three days of moving into your Vienna address.

entity_title: Residence registration (Meldezettel) within three days — third-country
fact_text: Anyone who takes up accommodation in a dwelling in Austria must register with the competent registration authority (residence registration / Meldezettel) within three days of moving into the accommodation.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: your residence permit is the only registration needed. Actually: separately, everyone taking up accommodation in Austria must file a residence registration (Meldezettel) with the registration authority within three days of moving in. Action required: file the Meldezettel within three days of moving into your Vienna address.

entity_title: Compulsory social insurance on taking up employment — EEA
fact_text: Social insurance in Austria comprises health, pension and accident insurance and is compulsory: as soon as you take up occupation you are automatically covered, your employer registers you with the social insurance institution and deducts contributions, and you receive a social insurance number and an e-card.
evidence_quote: As soon as a person takes up occupation they are automatically covered by insurance.

entity_title: Compulsory social insurance on taking up employment — third-country

entity_title: Tax residency (over six months) and unlimited taxation — EEA
fact_text: If you spend more than six months of the year in Austria (staying overnight during the working week), you can be considered ordinarily resident in Austria and are then subject to unlimited taxation in Austria — i.e. taxed on your worldwide income.
evidence_quote: If the worker concerned stays overnight in Austria (at least part of the time) during the working week, and if they spend more than six months of the year in Austria, they can be considered to be ordinarily resident in Austria and therefore subject to unlimited taxation in Austria.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: Austria only taxes your Austrian salary. Actually: spending more than six months in Austria makes you ordinarily resident and subject to unlimited taxation, which covers worldwide income. Action required: track your days and check the applicable double-taxation treaty.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen: apply for an EU residence document for stays over 3 months
fact_text: As a citizen of an EU/EEA country or Switzerland you must apply for an EU residence document if you stay in Denmark for more than 3 months, and you must apply before the three months expire (jobseekers have up to 6 months); Nordic citizens do not need one.
evidence_quote: Citizens of EU, EEA countries and Switzerland have to apply for an EU residence document if they stay for more than 3 months.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: an EU citizen just moves to Denmark with no paperwork. Actually: for stays over three months you must apply for an EU residence document (registration certificate) before the three months expire; note Nordic citizens are exempt. Action required: apply to SIRI in Copenhagen soon after arrival.

entity_title: EU residence document is needed before you can register an address and get a CPR number
fact_text: As an EU citizen you need your EU residence document before you can register a Danish address with the municipality and receive a Danish CPR number.
evidence_quote: You therefore need an EU residence document before you can register an address and receive a Danish CPR number.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you can get a CPR number as soon as you arrive. Actually: as an EU citizen you must first obtain your EU residence document, because it is required before you can register your address and be given a CPR number. Action required: sequence the EU residence document first, then CPR registration.

entity_title: Non-EU/EEA nationals need a residence and work permit
fact_text: As a citizen from outside the EU/EEA, the Nordic region or Switzerland, you need a residence and work permit to live and work in Denmark.
evidence_quote: Residence and work permit (relevant if you are a citizen outside the EU/EEA, the Nordic region or Switzerland)

entity_title: Pay Limit Scheme: residence and work permit for a high-salary job (third-country)
fact_text: As a non-EU/EEA national offered a job in Denmark with a high salary you can apply for a residence and work permit under the Pay Limit Scheme; the salary must be at least the annually-regulated minimum amount (DKK 552,000 per year in 2026).
evidence_quote: You have been offered a job in Denmark with a salary of DKK 552,000 or higher.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: any job offer qualifies a non-EU worker for a Danish permit. Actually: the widely-used Pay Limit Scheme requires a salary at or above an annually-set minimum (DKK 552,000 in 2026), regardless of your field or hours. Action required: check the offered salary against the current minimum amount.

entity_title: CPR number and civil registration (Folkeregistret) — EEA
fact_text: Everyone in Denmark has a CPR (civil registration) number, essential for dealings with the authorities and for tax and social security; if you intend to stay 3 months or more (6 months if within EU/EEA or Nordic countries) you must notify the Civil Registration Office (Folkeregistret), and a permanent Danish address is mandatory to obtain a CPR number.
evidence_quote: If you intend to stay for a period of 3 months or more (6 months if within EU/EEA or Nordic countries) you must notify the Civil Registration Office (Folkeregistret).

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you get a personal number automatically. Actually: you must actively notify the Civil Registration Office (Folkeregistret) — as an EU/EEA citizen once your stay reaches 6 months — and you can only get a CPR number once you have a permanent Danish address. Action required: register with the municipality to obtain your CPR number.

entity_title: National health insurance card ('the yellow card' / sundhedskort) — EEA
fact_text: The Danish national health insurance card ('the yellow card' / sundhedskort) documents your entitlement to services under the national health insurance scheme; it is issued when you register for a CPR number at (International) Citizen Service and is sent to your Danish address about 2 to 3 weeks later.
evidence_quote: The health insurance card is issued when you register for a CPR number with Citizen Service in your municipality or in one of the International Citizen Service centres.

entity_title: Full tax liability and worldwide income — EEA
fact_text: If you are resident in Denmark or stay for 6 consecutive months you have full tax liability, meaning as a general rule all your earned income — including salary and capital income from outside Denmark — is subject to taxation in Denmark.
evidence_quote: Full tax liability means that as a general rule all your earned income (salary and income from capital - also from outside Denmark) is subject to taxation in Denmark. To be fully liable to pay tax to Denmark you must either stay in Denmark for 6 months consecutively or be resident in Denmark.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: Denmark only taxes your Danish salary. Actually: becoming resident (or staying six consecutive months) triggers full tax liability on worldwide income, including foreign salary and capital income. Action required: check the applicable double-taxation treaty and your move date.
